name: Parcel redelivery fee text (UK)
audience: everyone, especially online shoppers and older parents
summary: A text or email pretends to be Royal Mail, Evri or DPD and says a parcel is held until you pay a small fee through a link. The link steals card details.
tells: Asks you to pay a redelivery, dispatch or 'unpaid postage' fee through a link (DPD says it never does this; Royal Mail leaves a grey 'Fee to Pay' card for underpaid post)
Sender is a random mobile number or email address instead of the courier's name
Link is not on the courier's real domain (royalmail.com, evri.com / evri.link, dpd.co.uk)
Shortened or odd-looking link, e.g. bit.ly or a long hyphenated domain
You were not expecting a parcel, or never asked for tracking updates
Pressure: 'parcel will be returned to sender today'
example: Royal Mail: Your parcel is on hold due to an unpaid shipping fee of £1.45. Pay before 23:59 to avoid return: hxxps://royalmail-redelivery[.]info/pay
aiAngle: Kits generate thousands of convincing lookalike domains and perfectly written texts, so spelling mistakes are no longer a reliable tell.

name: USPS package tracking text
audience: everyone in the US, online shoppers
summary: A text claims USPS cannot deliver a package because of an incomplete address or unpaid fee, and sends you to a fake site to 'update' details and pay.
tells: Unsolicited text about a delivery problem (USPS says it does not text you unless you requested tracking, and those texts have no link)
Link to a domain that is not usps.com
Asks for card details or a small redelivery payment
Tells you to reply 'Y' and reopen the message to activate the link
Urgent deadline such as 'within 12 hours'
example: USPS: Your package could not be delivered due to an incomplete address. Update within 12 hours: hxxps://usps-redelivery-center[.]com/track (Reply Y then reopen this message to activate the link)
aiAngle: Smishing kits sold as a service let one crew run thousands of fresh domains a day, outpacing blocklists.

name: Missed delivery / reschedule email
audience: everyone
summary: An email says a courier tried to deliver and you must 'reschedule' or confirm details via a link or attachment, leading to a fake login, card form or malware.
tells: Generic greeting like 'Dear Customer'
Attachment (zip, html, pdf) you are told to open to see 'delivery details'
Asks you to log in or enter card details to rebook
Sender address does not end in the courier's real domain
No real tracking number, or one that does not work on the courier's own site
example: We missed you! Your parcel DX-48213 could not be delivered today. Choose a new delivery slot here: hxxps://dhl-reschedule-portal[.]net/rebook
aiAngle: AI writes fluent, branded emails in any language, so poor grammar is rarer.

name: "Hi Mum/Dad, new number"
audience: parents and grandparents
summary: A message from an unknown number claims to be your child with a broken or lost phone, then asks you to urgently pay a bill or lend money.
tells: Unknown number starting 'Hi Mum' or 'Hi Dad' without using a name
Claims their phone is broken, lost or 'this is my new number'
Quickly asks for money for an urgent bill, often to someone else's account
Gives a reason they cannot call or voice note right now
Asks you to keep it quick or not tell anyone
example: Hi Mum it's me, dropped my phone down the loo so this is my new number. Can you save it? Also I've got a bill I need to pay today but my banking app won't work on this phone x
aiAngle: Scammers can follow up with an AI voice clone of the child, made from a few seconds of social media audio.

audience: everyone, especially older adults
summary: Someone posing as your bank's fraud team (or the police) says your account is under attack and talks you into moving money to a 'safe account' they control.
tells: Asks you to move money to a 'safe' or 'holding' account (banks never do this)
Caller ID or text appears in your bank's real message thread (spoofing)
Asks for a one-time passcode, PIN or full password
Tells you not to speak to branch staff or family
Text about a 'new payee' or suspicious payment followed by a call
Pressure to act before you can hang up and check
example: NatWest: A payment of £1,250.00 to a new payee was attempted from your account. If this was NOT you, call our fraud team immediately on 0203 000 0000.

Link domain looks like Discord but is not discord.com or discord.gg (e.g. dlscord, discord-gift, discordnitro)
Asks you to log in again or scan a QR code to 'claim'
Message is copy-pasted and posted in many channels at once

tells: Urgent deadline: 'confirm within 24 hours or your booking is cancelled'
Asks for card details or a payment that is not in the payment policy on your booking confirmation
Link goes to a site that does not end in booking.com
Asks you to move the conversation to WhatsApp, text or email
Asks for a bank transfer or gift cards (Booking.com says no real payment needs gift cards)
example: Dear guest, your reservation at Hotel Aurora (12-15 May) is at risk. Our bank could not verify your card. Please re-confirm within 24h to avoid cancellation: hxxps://booking-guest-verify[.]com/r/48213
aiAngle: Criminals use real booking details and AI-written messages in the guest's own language, so the message reads exactly like the hotel.

name: 'Receive your payment' link for sellers (OLX, Vinted, Kleinanzeigen)
audience: teens and adults selling second-hand items on Vinted, OLX, Allegro, Kleinanzeigen, Marktplaats or Leboncoin
summary: A 'buyer' says they have already paid through the platform's safe delivery and sends a link so you can 'receive the money'. The page copies your real listing, then asks for your card or online banking login and SMS codes.
tells: Buyer agrees instantly without asking questions, then wants to move to WhatsApp, text or email
Says payment is waiting and you must click a link to 'receive', 'confirm' or 'unlock' it
Page shows your real item and photo but is not on the marketplace's own domain
Asks for your card number, CVC, bank login or an SMS code to 'receive' money
Sends a payment 'screenshot' as proof (easy to fake)
Money never appears in the real app or your bank account
example: Hi! I bought your jacket with Vinted secure delivery. The courier is booked, you just need to confirm to receive €45: hxxps://vinted-receive-funds[.]eu/item/77310
aiAngle: Scam kits auto-generate a fake 'payment received' page from your real listing in seconds, in any language.

name: Bank 'suspicious payment' text then fake bank call (EU)
audience: everyone with a bank or fintech app, especially N26, ING, Revolut and Sparkasse customers
summary: A text says there is a suspicious payment or your account is blocked and gives a link to 'verify'. The link copies your bank's login page. Then a fake bank agent may call to get you to approve a payment or share a code in your app.
tells: Text with a link about a blocked account or a payment you did not make (N26 says it never sends links by SMS)
Time pressure or an ultimatum to log in now
Login page is not your bank's real address (the bank name inside a URL does not make it real)
A call soon after from 'your bank' that knows your name, and the caller ID may even match the real bank
Caller asks you to read out an SMS code or approve a payment or new device in your app
Asks you to install an app or 'security update' from a link
example: N26: A payment of €489.00 to an electronics store is waiting for approval. Not you? Cancel it here: hxxps://n26-secure-cancel[.]com
aiAngle: Spoofed caller ID and AI voice tools make the follow-up 'bank' call sound and look official.

name: One-ring missed call from a foreign number (Wangiri)
audience: everyone with a mobile phone
summary: Your phone rings once from an unusual international number and stops. If you call back, you are connected to an expensive premium-rate line and charged for the call.
tells: Missed call that rang only once
Unusual international country code you do not recognise
Comes at night or during working hours when you are unlikely to answer
No voicemail left (a real caller would leave a message or ring again)
example: Missed call (1 ring) from +375 XX XXX XXXX at 02:14. No voicemail.

name: Tax refund or tax debt message (EU)
audience: adults who file taxes, and parents
summary: A message pretends to be the tax office (Revenue, impots.gouv.fr, Belastingdienst, Finanzamt and others) and says you are owed a refund, or must pay a tax bill now, through a link or QR code. The page steals card or bank details.
tells: Refund or debt announced by text or email with a link (Revenue Ireland says it never tells you about a refund or bill by email, SMS or phone)
Asks for your card number to receive a refund (the French tax office says it never asks for it)
Direct payment link or QR code to pay a tax debt (Belastingdienst says it never sends direct payment requests)
Threats of bailiffs, seizure or police if you do not pay today
Link not on the real tax site (revenue.ie, impots.gouv.fr, belastingdienst.nl, elster.de)
example: impots.gouv.fr: Après recalcul, vous avez droit à un remboursement de 312,40 €. Confirmez vos coordonnées bancaires avant le 30/09: hxxps://impots-remboursement-fr[.]info
aiAngle: AI translation lets one gang run the same refund scam against tax offices in many countries at once, with correct local wording.

name: Boss or colleague asking for gift cards
audience: employees, volunteers, club and church members
summary: A message that looks like it's from your manager, a colleague or a club leader asks for a quick favour: buy gift cards and send photos of the codes. The real person never sent it.
tells: Asks for gift cards (Apple, Google Play, Amazon, Steam) and photos of the codes
Says they're in a meeting and can't talk, so you can't check
Urgent 'quick favour' with a promise to pay you back
Comes from a new number or a personal email address, not their usual one
example: Are you at your desk? I need a quick favour, I'm in a meeting and can't talk. Can you get 4 Apple gift cards of £100 for a client and send me photos of the codes? I'll pay you back today. - Sarah
aiAngle: AI makes it easy to copy a boss's writing style from public posts and emails.

name: Streaming or subscription 'payment failed'
audience: anyone with Netflix, Disney+, Spotify, Amazon Prime or similar
summary: A message says your Netflix (or another subscription) payment failed and your account is on hold. The link goes to a fake login and card page.
tells: Says your account is suspended or on hold because a payment failed
Link to a site that isn't the service's real address
Asks you to re-enter card details through the link
Deadline like 24 or 48 hours before the account is closed
example: Netflix: We couldn't process your last payment. Your account is on hold. Update your billing details within 24 hours to avoid cancellation: hxxps://netflix-billing-update[.]com
aiAngle: Phishing kits copy the real login page pixel for pixel, so the page itself looks right.
